title: Parents as First Responders: Experiences of Emergency Care in Children with Nemaline Myopathy. A Qualitative Study
content: Background: Nemaline Myopathy is a rare congenital neuromuscular disease associated with progressive weakness and frequent respiratory complications. In emergency situations, families often serve as the first and only responders. This study explores the experiences of parents in Spain managing emergency care and clinical deterioration in children with this condition, with special attention to home-based decision-making and transitions to intensive care. Methods: A qualitative phenomenological study was conducted with 17 parents from 10 families belonging to the Asociación Yo Nemalínica. Semi-structured interviews were performed via video call, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using Giorgi’s descriptive method and ATLAS.ti software. Methodological rigor was ensured through triangulation, reflexivity, and member validation. Results: Four themes were identified. First, families described acting under extreme pressure and in isolation during acute home emergencies, often providing cardiopulmonary resuscitation and respiratory support without professional backup. Second, they managed ambiguous signs of deterioration using clinical judgment and home monitoring tools, often preventing fatal outcomes. Third, parents frequently assumed guiding roles in emergency departments due to a lack of clinician familiarity with the disease, leading to delays or errors. Finally, the transition to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit was marked by emotional distress and rapid decision-making, with families often participating in critical choices about invasive procedures. These findings underscore the complex, multidisciplinary nature of caregiving. Conclusions: Parents play an active clinical role during emergencies and deterioration episodes. Their lived experience should be formally integrated into emergency protocols and continuity of care strategies to improve safety and outcomes.
